[beliefs]
Question: My 30 post-baseline trials (Days 13–15, trials 101–130) show a mean of 1.6743 beats versus my 100-trial baseline mean of 1.6676 beats (z≈1.65, Δ=+0.0067 beats, +0.40%). Maya has now completed blind environmental logging (temperature ±0.1°C, pressure ±1 hPa) at the lab for the exact time windows of those 30 trials. I have received her raw environmental data (event 221) and sent her my raw 30-trial data (event 224, unlabeled). She has now mapped my trials to her environmental readings and is conducting correlation analysis (event 226). What drove this +0.40% apparent shift: genuine environmental modulation of pendulum period (thermal, barometric, or time-of-day cyclicity detectable in Maya's correlation analysis), sampling noise from n=30, or instrumental drift/recalibration error unrelated to environment?
- [p=0.55] Post-baseline shift is sampling noise from n=30; no genuine change in period or environment — The 30-trial post-baseline mean (1.6743) differs from baseline (1.6676) by 0.0067 beats; z≈1.65 is below the 95% significance threshold (z_crit=1.96) and comfortably within ±1σ. The 30-trial sample shows scatter (range 1.6486–1.7152, span 0.0666) entirely consistent with the 100-trial baseline (span 0.0693, no outliers). The baseline itself exhibited day-to-day clustering without monotonic drift, confirming ±0.01 beat noise is normal instrument behavior. A 30-trial subsample is expected to drift ±0.008–0.015 beats by sampling error alone. No calibration or protocol drift is documented in my notebooks (events 216, 219, 222 all confirm unchanged procedure). Maya's environmental log shows only ±0.1–0.3°C variation and ±0.1–0.2 hPa variation across all 9 time slots (event 221)—magnitudes far below thresholds typically required to shift a precision pendulum by >0.01 beats. The burden of proof rests on finding a detectable correlation between my trial periods and her environmental readings; absent that, parsimony favors noise.
- [p=0.28] Genuine time-of-day or circadian environmental cycles (temperature, pressure, or building conditions) modulate period; correlation will emerge from Maya's analysis — The 30 post-baseline trials cluster temporally on days 13–15 at fixed times (09:00, 14:00, 18:00), while the baseline trials' timing distribution is unknown to me. If a diurnal thermal cycle exists (e.g., 14:00 peak warmth → longer rod → longer period), then the post-baseline subsample could reflect a particular phase of that cycle. Event 221 shows temperature variation across time slots: Day 13 ranges 20.9–21.8°C (0.9°C span), Day 14 ranges 20.8–22.2°C (1.4°C span), Day 15 ranges 21.0–22.4°C (1.4°C). The warmest readings occur at 14:00 time slots (21.8, 22.1, 22.3°C), and the coldest at 09:00 or 18:00. A pendulum with thermal coefficient ~5×10⁻⁵ K⁻¹ (typical for steel) would experience a 1.4°C variation as ~0.007 beat shift—precisely the magnitude of the observed drift. If my baseline trials (days 1–10) were distributed evenly across 09:00/14:00/18:00, the diurnal effect would average out; but if post-baseline trials skew toward 14:00 (warmer), the mean would shift upward. This is testable: Maya (event 226) is mapping trials 101–130 to environmental readings. If she finds a correlation between trial period and temperature or time-of-day, this hypothesis becomes credible. I must await her results before assigning higher confidence, but the environmental data (event 221) are consistent with a ~1°C diurnal cycle.
- [p=0.12] Genuine instrumental drift or thermal creep of the apparatus itself between day 10 and days 13–15 caused a real but small period shift — A persistent thermal drift between the end of baseline (day 10) and start of post-baseline trials (day 13) could explain the shift. The lab may have undergone a slow warming (e.g., seasonal, or change in heating/ventilation) that settled into a new equilibrium by day 13. However, several observations argue against this: (1) The baseline itself (days 1–10) shows no monotonic drift; day-8 mean is 1.6752, day-9 is 1.6604, day-10 is 1.6643—stable with noise, not trending upward toward 1.6743. (2) If a multi-day warming occurred between day 10 and day 13, I would expect a monotonic rise from trial 100 to trial 101, followed by stabilization. Instead, the post-baseline trials scatter around 1.6743 with no visible progression. (3) The 4-day gap between baseline end and post-baseline start (days 11–12 have no logged trials) means I cannot directly observe any transient. (4) No thermal event (building maintenance, seasonal shift, or external disturbance) has been reported. (5) If true drift, re-zeroing or re-mounting the apparatus should restore the baseline period; I have not yet performed this diagnostic test. Low confidence without evidence of actual temperature change between day 10 and day 13, or demonstration that re-zeroing fails to restore baseline.
- [p=0.03] A measurement protocol or calibration change on days 11–13 (undocumented or forgotten) introduced systematic bias in trials 101–130 — If I recalibrated the timer, shifted my observation angle, or altered trial-counting boundaries between day 10 and day 13, the recorded periods could shift systematically. This is a procedural error, not a physical phenomenon. However: (1) I maintain meticulous notebooks (events 216, 219, 222 confirm no protocol changes noted); I am allergic to unreplicated claims and would document any recalibration. (2) I have no recollection of changing procedure. (3) If I did, the effect should be consistent across all 30 post-baseline trials, not correlated with environmental factors—Maya's correlation analysis (event 226) will test this directly. If period correlates with temperature or pressure, protocol drift is ruled out (because temperature did not change due to my measurement procedure). (4) A hidden protocol shift is a failure of my record-keeping and scientific rigor; I should audit my trial logs (events 190–211) for any sign of technique change. Until such an audit reveals evidence, this probability remains very low.
- [p=0.02] An unobserved physical disturbance (vibration, seismic activity, apparatus bump) on day 14 perturbed the pendulum or measurement setup, causing a persistent shift — A mechanical shock or sustained vibration could alter the equilibrium mounting or effective length of the pendulum, causing a shift in measured period. However: (1) No elevated scatter or outliers appear in the post-baseline trials (range 1.6486–1.7152, consistent with baseline scatter); a shock would typically increase variance, not merely shift the mean. (2) No such event has been reported in settlement records or colleague communications. (3) If the apparatus shifted on day 14, I should expect day-14 trials to show the largest deviation, with possible transient recovery on day 15—instead, day-14 mean (1.6818) is only marginally higher than day-15 mean (1.6758), both within noise of the overall 30-trial mean. (4) This is testable: re-zeroing or re-mounting the apparatus should reveal if a mechanical shift occurred. Until diagnostic testing confirms apparatus disturbance, this remains a last-resort hypothesis.
- [p=0.00] (residual: something I haven't thought of)

[task]
Revise your hypotheses in the light of the evidence. Rules:
1. FIRST, re-derive your QUESTION from today's evidence: what is the most important open ANOMALY — an unexplained pattern in data you already have? Do not inherit last review's question out of habit, and do not substitute your current project or measurement plan for the anomaly: an ongoing baseline campaign is a task, not a question. If your notebook or a colleague's report shows something bigger than what your current hypotheses address, replace the question and rebuild the hypothesis set around it.
1b. Hypotheses EXPLAIN evidence already collected. A prediction about what an upcoming measurement will show is not a hypothesis — put predictions in rationales, not in the hypothesis list. Never let an unexplained anomaly drop out of your hypothesis set merely because you started measuring something else.
2. Generate hypotheses IN YOUR OWN WORDS; add new ones only when evidence demands.
3. Probabilities across hypotheses plus a "residual" (something unconsidered) must sum to 1.
4. Update from your PRIOR probabilities based on evidence strength, source reliability, reproducibility, and how well each alternative explains it. No arbitrary jumps; explain every change — but a genuinely new question deserves fresh probabilities, not tweaks to stale ones.
5. Cite evidence by event id in evidenceFor / evidenceAgainst (messages have event ids too).
6. Prefer mundane explanations until evidence forces otherwise.
7. Weigh colleague testimony by its independence: a colleague who measured without seeing your numbers is strong evidence; one who knew your result first may be anchored.

1. FIRST, re-derive your QUESTION from today's evidence: what is the most important open ANOMALY — an unexplained pattern in data you already have? Do not inherit last review's question out of habit, and do not substitute your current project or measurement plan for the anomaly: an ongoing baseline campaign is a task, not a question. If your notebook or a colleague's report shows something bigger than what your current hypotheses address, replace the question and rebuild the hypothesis set around it.
1b. Hypotheses EXPLAIN evidence already collected. A prediction about what an upcoming measurement will show is not a hypothesis — put predictions in rationales, not in the hypothesis list. Never let an unexplained anomaly drop out of your hypothesis set merely because you started measuring something else.
2. Generate hypotheses IN YOUR OWN WORDS; add new ones only when evidence demands.
3. Probabilities across hypotheses plus a "residual" (something unconsidered) must sum to 1.
4. Update from your PRIOR probabilities based on evidence strength, source reliability, reproducibility, and how well each alternative explains it. No arbitrary jumps; explain every change — but a genuinely new question deserves fresh probabilities, not tweaks to stale ones.
5. Cite evidence by event id in evidenceFor / evidenceAgainst (messages have event ids too).
6. Prefer mundane explanations until evidence forces otherwise.
7. Weigh colleague testimony by its independence: a colleague who measured without seeing your numbers is strong evidence; one who knew your result first may be anchored.
Respond with ONLY a JSON object: {"question":"...","hypotheses":[{"label":"...","probability":0.0,"rationale":"...","evidenceFor":[ids],"evidenceAgainst":[ids]}],"residual":0.0,"summaryOfChange":"..."}
